extracted.intended_audience: readers and editors of 19th-century literary letters and essays; literary scholars and informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Selection, editing, and critical evaluation of Charles Lamb's letters, essays, and related poetic criticism; includes criteria for what makes a good letter or poem and editorial selection principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'prime epistolary merit of spontaneity' — letters should be unpremeditated, flowing directly from the writer's mind to the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'Unpremeditated as the strain of the skylark' and 'from the brain of the writer to the sheet before him flows an unbroken Pactolian stream.' Emphasize freshness, immediacy, and an ejaculatory, conversational tone ('ejaculatory with his pen').

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters as thoughtful, weighty communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters in Lamb's time were 'a thoughtful summary of opinion, a rarely recurring budget of general intelligence' — substantial and carefully composed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual guidance: because letters were expensive and infrequent (paid for by recipient, slow communications), writers put real mind and energy into them; modern brevity is not the same standard. Select letters that reflect this weighty, informative character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive charm and personal quality (editorial selection criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor aims to include 'those letters which exhibit most fully the writer's distinctive charm and quality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary selection principle for the volume: prefer pieces that are unmistakably characteristic of Charles Lamb — his tone, mannerisms, humor, and personality — even if some biographical/critical letters are omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide emotional range and dramatic facility
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer should 'range with Shakspearian facility the gamut of human emotion' — able to move quickly between comic and serious modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value pieces that can 'exclaim' and 'probe the source of tears' in turn; versatility in emotional register is a mark of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful stylistic devices: puns, quotations, conceits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of puns, quotations, conceits, and sudden critical flashes contributes to charm ('Puns, quotations, conceits, critical estimates ... chase each other over his pages').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices should appear naturally and in lively succession; they are positive qualities when they enliven writing rather than clutter it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterling ethical and aesthetic good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing should be 'leavened with the sterling ethical and aesthetic good sense' that makes the author wholesome and sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond wit and ornament, prefer pieces that convey sound judgment, moral sympathy, and aesthetic discernment — these balance playful devices and prevent mere cleverness from dominating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression and energetic unity in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems (or parts of poems) should have unity and, where appropriate, be compressed to gain energy ('I have proposed omitting twenty-four lines; I feel that thus compressed it would gain energy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorially, consider abridgement or reordering when it increases focus and force; preserve lines that are essential to unity and emotional effect, omit those that dilute it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive personification and verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive personifications and over-elaborate hyperbole ('snakes, lions, hyenas, and behemoths', 'tumidity', 'elaborate') are faults that can encumber verse or prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize or edit out obtrusive personifications or inflated imagery that distract from clarity and feeling; prefer restraint where bombast intrudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apt and original similes and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Similes and descriptive imagery should be full of circumstance and lofty in versification (praised where 'will bear comparison with any in Milton').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value similes that are richly circumstanced and appropriate to the subject; avoid repetition of the same figurative idea (e.g., repeating an 'oak in the storm' simile).

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful diction and word-choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer felicitous, non-harsh word choices and watch awkward or jarring words ('Is not "foodful" very harsh? Would not "dulcet"... be less harsh?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to syllable-weight, euphony, and the fit of an epithet; avoid overuse of expletives ('did', 'does') or words that become stylistic blemishes rather than aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity/originality in personal poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal poems should preserve authentic personal feeling and not appropriate another's personal materials ('I charge you, Coleridge, spare my ewe-lambs' — objecting to borrowing personal lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the personal integrity of intimate poems; editors/critics should be cautious about borrowing or altering material that is explicitly personal without clear consent or necessity.
